title: Indian Physicist Deepak Dhar Wins 2026 Dirac Medal, Joining Hawking and Witten in Elite Physics Pantheon
excerpt: The IISER Pune professor becomes the first Indian-born scientist to receive the ICTP Dirac Medal, awarded alongside three co-laureates for pioneering work in statistical mechanics and AI.
body:
• Deepak Dhar, 74, wins the 2026 ICTP Dirac Medal alongside Bernard Derrida, Marc Mézard, and Haim Sompolinsky for contributions to statistical mechanics and its applications in AI.
  • Dhar is the first Indian-born physicist to receive the prestigious medal, which has been a precursor to Nobel Prizes for eight previous laureates.
  • He previously became the first Indian to win the Boltzmann Medal in 2022 and received the Padma Bhushan in 2023.
  • The award recognizes work that has extended statistical mechanics into non-equilibrium systems, optimization problems, theoretical neuroscience, and artificial intelligence.

A Historic First for Indian Physics

Deepak Dhar, an Indian theoretical physicist based at the International Centre for Theoretical Sciences (ICTS-TIFR) in Bengaluru, has been named a co-recipient of the 2026 ICTP Dirac Medal — one of the most prestigious awards in theoretical physics. He shares the honor with Bernard Derrida of France, Marc Mézard of France, and Haim Sompolinsky of Israel.

https://x.com/IndiaToday/status/2086482396015374366

The four were recognized "for their pioneering contributions to equilibrium statistical mechanics and for extending its concepts and methods into non-equilibrium statistical mechanics, optimization problems, theoretical neuroscience, and, finally, artificial intelligence," according to the International Centre for Theoretical Physics (ICTP) in Trieste, Italy.

The medal, awarded annually on August 8 — the birthday of physicist Paul Dirac — places Dhar in the company of some of the greatest minds in modern physics. Eight previous Dirac Medallists have gone on to win Nobel Prizes, including luminaries such as Edward Witten, who also won the Fields Medal.

"Scientists are like children playing on the sea shore. They look for pebbles and for nice sea shells. Some of them manage to find better sea shells than others. And that is how I feel. Maybe I was lucky to have found some nice problems to work on."

— Deepak Dhar, at his Boltzmann Medal felicitation

From Pratapgarh to the Pinnacle of Physics

Born on October 30, 1951, in Pratapgarh, Uttar Pradesh, Dhar studied at the University of Allahabad and IIT Kanpur before earning his PhD from the California Institute of Technology under Jon Mathews. He returned to India to join the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR) in Mumbai, where he spent the bulk of his career before moving to the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research (IISER) in Pune and later to ICTS-TIFR in Bengaluru.

His research in statistical physics and stochastic processes has been foundational. His work on self-organized criticality models, interfacial growth, and percolation problems helped establish frameworks that other physicists and mathematicians have built upon for decades.

Statistical Mechanics Meets Artificial Intelligence

The citation's mention of artificial intelligence underscores how the four laureates' work has bridged pure physics and emerging technology. The mathematical frameworks developed for understanding complex systems — from spin glasses to neural networks — now underpin key advances in machine learning and deep learning architectures. Haim Sompolinsky's work on theoretical neuroscience, for instance, has directly influenced how researchers model neural computation, while Mézard's contributions to optimization problems have shaped algorithmic design.

For Dhar, the recognition reflects decades of quiet, methodical work. Currently serving as INSA Distinguished Professor, he continues research at the intersection of mathematical physics and complex systems theory.

What the Diaspora Angle Means

Dhar's achievement resonates strongly within the Indian scientific community and diaspora. Unlike many Indian-origin scientists who have built careers abroad, Dhar has spent the majority of his working life at Indian institutions — TIFR, IISER Pune, and ICTS-TIFR Bengaluru. His trajectory demonstrates that world-class theoretical physics can be conducted from India, a narrative that carries weight as the country invests more heavily in basic science research.

Looking Ahead

The formal medal ceremony is expected later this year at ICTP in Trieste. Given the track record — eight Dirac Medallists have subsequently won Nobel Prizes — the physics community will be watching Dhar's career trajectory with renewed attention. At 74, his body of work now stands among the most decorated in the history of Indian science.
